reconcile.connective: Commentators answer that Saul's slaughter left survivors and that "Agagite" is a dynastic label, so a later Amalekite of Agag's line is unsurprising though unprovable.

discrepancy.connective: The critical objection, pressed by L. B. Paton, is that Esther is an unhistorical festival novella in which "the Agagite" is a literary echo of 1 Samuel 15 rather than a real genealogy, so the two passages do not describe one continuous history.

excerpts.excerpt_text: For it follows from the very nature of the case that many escaped, and consequently there is nothing striking in the fact that Amalekites are mentioned again at a later period (Sa1 27:8; Sa1 30:1; Sa2 8:12).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the herem-was-total premise: the ban left survivors, so the line of Amalek (and so an Agagite) could persist into Persian times.

excerpts.excerpt_text: whom both the Targums make to descend from Amalek, and to be of the stock or family of Agag, the common name of the kings of Amalek … but this is not clear and certain
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Treats Haman's claimed descent from Agag as a tradition, not an asserted fact, deflating the assumption that Esther 3:1 affirms an unbroken Agag line.

excerpts.excerpt_text: This is certainly possible, though it can by no means be proved. … In 1 Sam 15, too, Agag is not the nomen propr. of the conquered king, but a general nomen dignitatis of the kings of Amalek, as Pharaoh and Abimelech were of the kings of Egypt and Gerar.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Makes the title-not-name move: 'Agag' is a dynastic title, so 'Agagite' need not mean descent from the specific Agag killed by Samuel, and the descent itself is unprovable.
